1.title: The Time Has Not Yet Come
1.context: Haggai's oracles are the most precisely dated in the prophets: four messages in four months of 520 BC, in Darius of Persia's second year. The first return from exile under Cyrus had happened sixteen years earlier; the temple foundation was laid then and the work had stalled, a story Ezra's book tells in full.
1.question: What have you been calling not yet time for, long after the reason expired?

1.title: Paneled Houses and a Pierced Bag
1.context: Paneling was a finish of settled, comfortable houses. The audit's five clauses all describe labor that almost suffices, and the refrain consider carefully your ways sounds twice in this chapter, the book's signature command.
1.question: Consider carefully your ways: which of the five clauses in this audit is closest to your own life right now?

1.title: Go Up into the Hills
1.context: The remedy is physical: timber from the hills and building on the site. Timber had to be hauled from Lebanon in Solomon's day, but the hills of Judah themselves could supply beams for this house.
1.question: What is the trip to the hills in front of you, the plain physical first step you have been postponing?

1.title: I Blew Away What You Brought Home
1.context: The lean years are interpreted by God Himself: the heavens withheld dew and the earth withheld crops on account of the ruined house and the busy private houses around it.
1.question: Where might a frustration in your ordinary work be a message about your priorities rather than about your effort?

1.title: A Drought Summoned
1.context: The oracle's inventory is total: fields, mountains, grain, wine, oil, man, beast, and all the labor of their hands. The first word ends without recording any reply; the answer comes in the next episode, with its own date.
1.question: What would it take for you to answer a hard word from God as quickly as this people is about to?

2.title: Governor, Priest, and Remnant Obeyed
2.context: The response names everyone the oracle addressed: Zerubbabel the governor, of David's line; Joshua the high priest; and all the remnant of the people. Fear of the LORD is the text's summary of their reply.
2.question: When a word from God lands on a whole community, what is your part in the obeying?

2.title: I Am with You
2.context: Haggai is titled here the messenger of the LORD, and the message he is introduced carrying is presence, not instruction. It is the shortest oracle in the book and the ground of everything built afterward.
2.question: What work in front of you would change if you believed I am with you was its foundation?

2.title: The LORD Stirred Their Spirits
2.context: Stirring is the word used of God waking Cyrus to issue the decree of return. Here it falls on governor, priest, and people at once: they obeyed, and God stirred, and the book keeps both verbs.
2.question: Where have you felt your own spirit stirred toward a work you had long left undone?

2.title: The Twenty-Fourth Day
2.context: Twenty-three days separate the rebuke from the first day of work. The book prints the date of the obedience as carefully as the date of the word, making the calendar itself part of the testimony.
2.question: What date could be written down, three weeks from now, for a work you begin because you considered your ways?

2.title: The Hinge of the Book
2.context: Five verses carry the whole turn of Haggai: rebuke answered, presence promised, work begun. The next word, a month into the building, will meet a different problem, discouragement, and is dated to the twenty-first day of the seventh month.
2.question: What short season of obedience in your past still encourages you when the work looks small?

3.title: Who Saw This House in Its Former Glory?
3.context: Solomon's temple had been destroyed sixty-six years before. The oldest builders could remember it from childhood, and the modest new work suffered by the comparison, a discouragement Ezra also records at the foundation laying.
3.question: What memory of a former glory makes your present work look like nothing, and is the comparison fair?

3.title: Be Strong, All You People of the Land
3.context: The triple be strong runs down the same chain as the obedience, governor, priest, people, and the promise underneath it reaches back to the exodus: My Spirit remains among you.
3.question: Which of the three words do you need most today: be strong, work, or do not be afraid?

3.title: I Will Shake the Nations
3.context: The shaking that once fell on Judah's fields is promised at the scale of the nations, and what it shakes loose is treasure for the house. The ground is ownership: the silver and gold already belong to God.
3.question: What treasure do you hold as if it were yours that this verse reassigns?

3.title: The Latter Glory Will Be Greater
3.context: The promise is comparative and future: greater than the former, with peace provided in this place. Faithful readers have understood the greater glory in more than one way, including the temple's later history and a glory still to come; the builders received it as a reason to keep building.
3.question: What promise are you building on whose fulfillment you will not live to measure?

3.title: A Question for the Priests
3.context: Two months later, on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, the word comes twice in one day. The first message begins not with a vision but with a legal question for the priests about how holiness and defilement travel.
3.question: Why do you think heaven teaches this next lesson through a ruling instead of a vision?

4.title: Holiness Does Not Travel, Defilement Does
4.context: Priests gave rulings, torah decisions, on questions of clean and unclean. Their two answers are asymmetric: consecrated meat does not sanctify what it touches, but corpse-defilement does spread by touch.
4.question: Where have you assumed goodness would rub off by proximity, when only defilement actually does?

4.title: Whatever They Offer There Is Defiled
4.context: Haggai applies the ruling to the nation: offerings at a neglected house did not cleanse the offerers, and the fields agreed, yielding half measures, ten for twenty and twenty for fifty, under blight, mildew, and hail.
4.question: What work of your hands might be carrying a defilement you have been treating as a technique problem?

4.title: From This Day On, I Will Bless You
4.context: The blessing is dated to the day the foundation was laid, the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, and pronounced in winter over an empty barn and bare vine, fig, pomegranate, and olive. From this day is the hinge phrase of the whole book.
4.question: Can you receive a blessing dated from today over fields that show no evidence of it yet?

4.title: I Will Overturn Royal Thrones
4.context: The day's second word is for Zerubbabel alone, and its scope is the thrones of the nations. The governor who had been handed a building project is told heaven is about to shake the political world around his little province.
4.question: What does it mean for your small assignment that God keeps the thrones in His own hand?

4.title: Like My Signet Ring
4.context: A signet ring was a king's personal seal. In Jeremiah 22, God tore the signet from Zerubbabel's grandfather Jehoiachin; here the grandson is made the signet, chosen. Zerubbabel is still called governor and servant, never king, and the book ends on the promise.
4.question: What family story of loss have you watched God quietly reverse in a later generation?
